concepts.heading: Understanding Consensual Non-Monogamy
concepts.alt: Three guides standing together smiling, each giving a thumbs up
concepts.plain: It means having more than one partner, and everyone knows and says yes.

concepts.heading: What CNM Is Not
concepts.alt: A guide holding a theatre mask away from his face, the mask crossed out by a red circle-slash
concepts.plain: It is not cheating. Cheating is hidden. This is out in the open.

concepts.heading: Dr. Elisabeth Sheff's Longitudinal Research
concepts.alt: A guide as a researcher with a clipboard and magnifying glass, studying a chart of connected hearts
concepts.plain: A researcher followed these families for many years. Most were doing fine.

concepts.heading: CNM as a Valid Relationship Orientation
concepts.plain: For some people this is simply how they love, not a phase.

concepts.heading: Addressing Common Misconceptions
concepts.alt: A guide popping a thought bubble that holds a question mark, using a pin
concepts.plain: Most of the scary things people say about it turn out to be untrue.

checks.prompt: Alex starts seeing someone new and hides it from their partner. Is that consensual non-monogamy?
checks.explanation: No, it is cheating. CNM is not cheating. Cheating involves deception — one or more partners are unaware of or have not agreed to outside connections.

checks.after: CNM as a Valid Relationship Orientation
checks.prompt: What makes a relationship consensually non-monogamous?
checks.explanation: Everyone involved knows and agrees. Consensual non-monogamy (CNM) refers to any relationship structure in which all partners knowingly and willingly agree that the relationship may include romantic, sexual, or intimate connections with more than one person.

f68fa226-1d2b-411c-b6c4-d0a1df5c1f85.takeaway: Having more than one partner is not cheating when everyone knows and agrees.

concepts.heading: Exploring Different CNM Structures
concepts.plain: There is no one right way to do this. You get to pick what fits.

concepts.heading: Polyamory
concepts.alt: Each holding a string of one big heart-shaped balloon
concepts.plain: Polyamory means loving more than one person, and everyone knows.

concepts.heading: Relationship Anarchy
concepts.alt: A guide drawing her own map of hearts and stars on a big sheet, a crossed-out ladder beside her
concepts.plain: You build each relationship your own way. No one type comes first by default.

concepts.heading: Open Relationships
concepts.alt: A couple holding hands, each using their free hand to open a door
concepts.plain: A couple agrees that one or both can also see other people.

concepts.heading: Swinging
concepts.alt: Two couples clinking glasses together at a party
concepts.plain: Couples who meet other couples or singles for sex, often as a social thing.

concepts.heading: Solo Polyamory
concepts.alt: A guide standing confidently on his own holding up a house key, small hearts orbiting him
concepts.plain: You have several partners but keep your own home and your own life.

concepts.heading: The RADAR Check-In System
concepts.alt: A guide watching a round radar screen that shows heart blips, clipboard in hand
concepts.plain: RADAR is a regular check-in with a set list of things to talk about.

concepts.heading: No Hierarchy of Validity
concepts.plain: No style is better than another. The best one is the one that works for you.

checks.prompt: Sam treats friends, lovers and partners as equally important and refuses to rank them. Which style is this?
checks.explanation: Relationship anarchy. Relationship anarchy, a concept developed by Andie Nordgren, rejects the idea that romantic or sexual relationships should automatically take precedence over friendships or other connections.

checks.prompt: Jordan has several loving relationships, lives alone and puts their own independence first. Which style is this?
checks.explanation: Solo polyamory. Solo polyamory describes people who maintain multiple relationships while prioritizing their own autonomy and independence.

828eaaa3-3922-4828-ad48-d46dc4194e52.takeaway: There are many ways to have more than one relationship. None is better than the others.

concepts.heading: Polysecure: Attachment Theory in CNM
concepts.plain: How safe you felt with people growing up shapes how you love now.

concepts.heading: Attachment Theory Basics
concepts.alt: A guide cradling a small glowing heart protectively, a tiny house icon above it
concepts.plain: People tend to get close in one of a few usual ways. These are learned early.

concepts.heading: Attachment in Polyamorous Contexts
concepts.alt: A guide holding a heart-rate style gauge whose needle swings high, looking surprised
concepts.plain: Having more partners can stir up old fears faster, not slower.

concepts.heading: The Concept of Nested Security
concepts.alt: Two guides standing inside three nested rings of light, like layers of shelter
concepts.plain: You need to feel safe in yourself, with each partner, and in the group.

concepts.heading: Building Security Across a Polycule
concepts.alt: Three guides passing a glowing heart between them in a triangle
concepts.plain: Feeling safe takes practice. Small, steady actions build it.

concepts.heading: Normalizing Attachment Struggles
concepts.plain: Struggling with this is normal. It does not mean you are broken.

checks.prompt: Fern says security in multi-partner relationships needs several layers of safety. What is that idea called?
checks.explanation: Nested security. Fern introduces the concept of "nested security" — the idea that secure attachment in CNM requires multiple layers of safety.

checks.prompt: In consensual non-monogamy, what tends to happen to attachment patterns?
checks.explanation: They become more activated. Fern argues that attachment styles become more activated in CNM contexts, not less.

83bd54a1-3422-4c24-a601-1ffdcf75fe5c.takeaway: Feeling safe with several partners is built on purpose, one steady action at a time.

concepts.heading: Ethics and Sustainability in CNM
concepts.plain: Doing this well means being honest and fair, again and again.

concepts.heading: Transparency and Honesty
concepts.alt: A guide holding an open glass jar with a glowing heart inside, nothing hidden
concepts.plain: Tell the truth about who you see and also how you feel.

concepts.heading: Rules vs. Agreements
concepts.alt: Two guides shaking hands over a shared sheet of paper, both smiling
concepts.plain: A rule is put on someone. An agreement is made together.

concepts.heading: Navigating Hierarchy, Veto Power, and Couple Privilege
concepts.alt: A guide standing on the top step of a small podium holding a stamp, looking down thoughtfully
concepts.plain: Watch out when one couple's comfort always beats everyone else's needs.

concepts.heading: Sheff's Research on Long-Term Success
concepts.alt: A guide watering a tall healthy plant whose leaves are hearts
concepts.plain: The people who last talk well, stay flexible and have support.

concepts.heading: Ethics of Disclosure
concepts.alt: He hands her an open envelope with a heart at the start of a path
concepts.plain: Tell new people how your relationships work before things get close.

concepts.heading: Continuous Growth
concepts.plain: You never finish learning this. You keep practising.

checks.prompt: Two partners talk it through and decide together how they will handle sleepovers. Is that a rule or an agreement?
checks.explanation: An agreement. Agreements are collaboratively created by all affected parties.

checks.prompt: When should you tell a new connection about your relationship structure?
checks.explanation: Early, before intimacy develops. When entering new connections, ethical practice requires disclosing your relationship structure early — before emotional or physical intimacy develops.

9c9d1cfb-4fec-4b13-8e23-9f7434d82d5c.takeaway: Be honest, make agreements together, and tell new people how your relationships work.
